processing: Standard sheng handling: withered, pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried, then pressed or sold as loose maocha, with no ripening pile.
harvest_season: Spring is the prized picking, as elsewhere in Yunnan; autumn tea is also made and sold cheaper.
appearance_dry: Slender, dark green twisted leaf with visible buds, as usual for Jingmai material.
appearance_liquor: Bright, clear pale gold when young.
appearance_wet: Supple mid-green leaves, smaller than those of many Xishuangbanna teas.
taste_profile: Local promotion speaks of orchid and honey, and Jingmai teas are generally known for fragrance; this particular village has no independent tasting record to add to that.

brewing.notes: Slightly cooler water than for a heavy Banna sheng helps keep the aroma clean, a common approach with Jingmai teas.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, mostly spring. Old-tree and younger-tree lots differ sharply in price: one published spring list gave 200 yuan/kg for small trees and 600 to 800 for old trees. Labels often say Jingmai rather than Mangjing, so ask which village the leaf came from.
description:
Mangjing is a Blang community on Jingmai Mountain in Lancang County, one of the two names (with Jingmai village) that the mountain's tea is usually sorted under. What sets it apart is the setting: old tea trees grown under forest cover around the villages.

The leaf is made the way other sheng is, sun-dried and then pressed or sold loose. The forest-grown material is what buyers pay for, not any special process.

The style usually attached to Jingmai is aromatic, with talk of orchid and honey and a moderate bitterness. Those are mountain-wide descriptions, so expect variation between Mangjing lots. Hot water and short steeps show the aroma; long steeps bring forward a bitter edge in young tea.

Buy with the tree age in mind, because the same village name covers cheap small-tree tea and much dearer old-tree tea. Blang people also make a traditional sour tea, usually fermented in sealed containers buried in the ground, which is a different thing from pressed sheng and worth trying if you find it.
history:
The Blang are said to have known the wild tea plant from around the 10th century, and with the Dai and other peoples developed growing tea beneath the forest canopy. That date comes from accounts of the mountain's heritage rather than from a record specific to Mangjing.

A provincial cooperative project on the Jingmai and Mangjing old tea gardens began in July 2002. In 2023 the Cultural Landscape of Old Tea Forests of the Jingmai Mountain in Pu'er was inscribed on the World Heritage List, the first tea-themed cultural site there, which brought much more attention to the villages.
